notes:
Now let me compile all the material into a verse-by-verse commentary. I have rich material from Enduring Word (charismatic/Pentecostal), Precept Austin (evangelical, aggregating multiple sources), Gill's Exposition (older Baptist-leaning), JFB (older evangelical), Matthew Henry, Morgan, Constable, Meyer, and others.

---

## 2 Chronicles 32 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — *After all these acts of faithfulness, Sennacherib king of Assyria came and invaded Judah...*

- **The surprising timing of the invasion.** After Hezekiah's extensive religious reforms (temple cleansing, covenant renewal, Passover revival, destruction of idolatry, reorganization of priesthood — see 2 Chronicles 29–31), Sennacherib invaded. This challenges a simplistic "obedience = immediate ease" theology. Faithfulness did not prevent the crisis; it preceded and prepared for it. The invasion becomes a test, not a punishment. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-32-commentary)
- G. Campbell Morgan notes: "It would seem to be a strange answer of God to the faithfulness of His child, that a strong foe should at this moment invade the kingdom; and yet how often the experience of the people of God is of this nature." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-32-commentary)
- Adam Clarke adds: "God did not permit the pious prince to be disturbed till he had completed the reformation which he had begun." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- David Guzik (Enduring Word) notes that the Chronicler omits the full story from 2 Kings 18:13-16 — that Hezekiah initially tried to buy Sennacherib off with temple gold, which failed. The Chronicler expects readers to know the Kings account and focuses on the theme of Yahweh's supremacy. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- JFB dates the invasion precisely to the 14th year of Hezekiah (701 BC) and notes Hezekiah had determined to recover Judah's independence by refusing the tribute his father Ahaz had bound the nation to pay to Assyria. (JFB: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-chronicles-32.html)
- Gill notes Hezekiah was in prosperous circumstances — he had defeated the Philistines, cast off the Assyrian yoke, and was well established in his throne. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- Bob Utley: "It is somewhat surprising that after Hezekiah's 'faithfulness' that Assyria attacked. Usually invasion was a result of covenant disobedience. Here, it was a way to reveal YHWH's power and uniqueness." (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-32-commentary)
- The Hebrew word for "faithfulness" is *'emeth* — not merely correct speech but faithful, sincere, inward reality before God. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-32-commentary)

---

### vv. 2–4 — *When Hezekiah saw that Sennacherib had come to make war against Jerusalem, he consulted with his leaders... about stopping up the waters...*

- This entire section (vv. 2-8) on Hezekiah's defensive preparations is **unique to Chronicles**, not found in 2 Kings or Isaiah. It is confirmed by Isaiah 22:8-11 and 2 Kings 20:20. (Ellicott, cited at https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- The stopping of springs was a common ancient Near Eastern defensive tactic — denying water to besiegers while securing it for the city. Hezekiah's plan was to cover the fountain heads so the enemy couldn't find them, and carry water by subterranean channels into the city. Jerusalem's water supply was vulnerable since it depended on two springs: Gihon in the Kidron valley and En-Rogel to the south. (JFB: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-chronicles-32.html and Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Gill notes the "brook that ran through the midst of the land" is identified by Kimchi (a medieval Jewish commentator) as Gihon (cf. v. 30). The stream was probably diverted into underground channels leading to reservoirs inside the city. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- The phrase "kings of Assyria" (plural) is rhetorical — though there was one king, he had tributary kings with him, and as he boasted, "my princes are altogether kings" (Isaiah 10:8). (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- Matthew Henry notes: "Those who trust God with their safety must use proper means, else they tempt him. God will provide, but so must we also." (Matthew Henry, cited at https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- F.B. Meyer emphasizes these preparations were "perfectly consistent with a true faith. Hezekiah's ultimate confidence was not in these things, but in that Greater One who was undoubtedly with them." (F.B. Meyer, cited at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/2-chronicles-32.html)
- Dr. Constable echoes: "It is no denial of one's trust in God if one makes certain precautionary preparations. 'Pray to God and keep your powder dry' is a wise response." (Constable, cited at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-32.html)

---

### v. 5 — *Then Hezekiah worked resolutely to rebuild all the broken sections of the wall... built an outer wall... produced an abundance of weapons and shields.*

- The "broken" wall likely refers to the section from the Gate of Ephraim to the Corner Gate, broken down by Joash king of Israel (2 Chronicles 25:23), possibly again damaged in Ahaz's time. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- Hezekiah built a second, outer wall. Josephus records that Jerusalem eventually had three walls. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- Selman notes that part of a wall likely from Hezekiah's time has been uncovered on Jerusalem's western hill — at seven metres thick, it is the thickest Iron Age wall known in Palestine, presumably designed to withstand Assyrian battering rams. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- JFB clarifies that "Millo" refers to the lower portion of Zion — "the original city of David" — and that the Hebrew reads better without the supplied preposition "in." It was this lower portion, not the whole city, that was repaired. (JFB: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-chronicles-32.html)

---

### vv. 6–8 — *Hezekiah appointed military commanders... gathered the people... encouraged them, saying, "Be strong and courageous!... With him is only the arm of flesh, but with us is the LORD our God..."*

- Hezekiah gathered the people "in the square of the city gate" — the large open space at the gate typical of Eastern cities, where public assemblies were held. (JFB: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-chronicles-32.html)
- His words "there is a greater One with us than with him" echo Elisha's words in 2 Kings 6:16. Clarke notes: "These words he quotes from the prophet Elisha… This was soon proved to be true by the slaughter made by the angel of the Lord." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- John Trapp sees in the phrase "with us is the LORD our God" the import of "Immanuel" (God with us), "by which name Christ now began to be known amongst them." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Gill notes that when Hezekiah said "there be more with us than with him," he meant not in numbers but in power and might — he had the Lord God in view. The Targum renders the phrase: "the Word of the Lord our God is for us to help us, and fight our battles." (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- The people "rested themselves upon the words of Hezekiah" — not on mere human rhetoric but on the substance: the strength and power of the Lord God he assured them was on their side. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)

---

### v. 9 — *Later, as Sennacherib... and all his forces besieged Lachish, he sent his servants to Jerusalem...*

- Lachish was 30 miles southwest of Jerusalem. Archaeologists have discovered a pit there with the remains of about 1,500 casualties of Sennacherib's attack. A wall relief from Sennacherib's palace in Nineveh (now in the British Museum) depicts the Assyrian king on a portable throne outside Lachish, with prisoners and booty passing by. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- The servants Sennacherib sent are identified in 2 Kings 18:17 as the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh — high-ranking Assyrian officials. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Gill notes this occurred after Hezekiah had given Sennacherib a large quantity of silver and gold to depart (2 Kings 18:14-16), and Sennacherib had withdrawn but then sent these messengers demanding surrender. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)

---

### vv. 10–12 — *"What is the basis of your confidence?... Is not Hezekiah misleading you...? Did not Hezekiah himself remove His high places...?"*

- The Assyrian rhetoric aimed to undermine trust — first in Hezekiah's leadership, then in God. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- In v. 12 the Assyrian displays profound theological misunderstanding: he assumes that removing the high places (local worship sites) would have angered Yahweh, since "more is always better." In reality, Hezekiah's reforms centralized worship at the one authorized altar in Jerusalem, pleasing God. This "demonic logic" is similar to how Satan twists obedience into something that looks like deprivation. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- F.B. Meyer observes: "There was considerable subtlety in Sennacherib's messages, but he did not understand how much that one altar meant, and how different Jehovah was from the idols of the nations." (F.B. Meyer, cited at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/2-chronicles-32.html)
- Grogan (Isaiah commentary) notes the theological misunderstanding in the field commander's speech argues for its authenticity, countering critics who call it a free creation by the biblical author. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- David Guzik notes the Assyrians also mocked Hezekiah's trust in an Egyptian alliance — a temptation Hezekiah indeed faced, which Isaiah strongly opposed (Isaiah 19, 20, 30). The Lord wanted Judah to trust Him, not Egypt. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)

---

### vv. 13–15 — *"Do you not know what I and my fathers have done...? Who among all the gods... has been able to deliver...? How much less will your God deliver you...?"*

- Sennacherib's argument is "simple and brilliant in its Satanic logic: 'The gods of other nations have not been able to protect them against us. Your God is just like one of them.'" (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- The Assyrian makes a fatal theological error: equating Yahweh with the idols of the nations. As Constable notes: "Sennacherib's fatal mistake was that he regarded Yahweh as only one of many idols. This was his undoing." (Constable, cited at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-32.html)
- Gill refers readers to his notes on Isaiah 36:18-20 for the parallel. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)

---

### vv. 16–19 — *And the servants of Sennacherib spoke further against the LORD God... He also wrote letters mocking the LORD... they called out loudly in Hebrew...*

- The Assyrians escalated from oral messages to written letters of blasphemy, and finally to shouting in Hebrew (the language of the common people, not the diplomatic Aramaic they were asked to use — Isaiah 36:11) to terrify the people on the wall. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/ and Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- Matthew Henry observes that the letters, "being more deliberate, is so much the worse." He also notes the servants "spoke yet more than he bade them against the Lord God and his servant Hezekiah. And God resents what is said against his servants, and will reckon for it, as well as what is said against himself." (Matthew Henry: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- v. 19 is the climactic blasphemy: they spoke against the God of Jerusalem "as against the gods of the people of the earth — the work of human hands." This is the tragic blindness — treating the living Creator as on par with manufactured idols. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- David Guzik notes: "For anyone who had the spiritual understanding to see it, Judah could have started planning the victory party right then, when the Assyrian... mocked the LORD God of Israel this way, and counted Him as 'just another god.'" (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)

---

### v. 20 — *In response, King Hezekiah and the prophet Isaiah son of Amoz cried out to heaven in prayer.*

- This verse — the joint prayer of king and prophet — is unique to Chronicles. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-32-commentary)
- Matthew Henry: "It was a happy time when the king and the prophet joined thus in prayer. Is any troubled? Is any terrified? Let him pray." He notes that praying to God is called "crying to heaven" because we eye Him as our Father in heaven. (Matthew Henry: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- F.B. Meyer: "It was the indignity done to Jehovah that stirred these two holy men to the heart… Oh that we were possessed with a similar zeal for God, so that we might look at sin as it affects Him, and lament over the awful wrongs which are continually being perpetrated against his holy, loving nature! What an argument this would give us in prayer!" (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- 2 Kings 19:14-15 gives the fuller picture: Hezekiah went into the house of the LORD and spread the blasphemous letter before God. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- **Ligonier (Reformed)** emphasizes that Hezekiah "could have chosen to resist Assyria in his own power or to continue relying on the alliance with Egypt, but he had a word from God through Isaiah to believe that the Lord would deliver him." The prayer shows that while God's promises are sure, we should not hesitate to pray after receiving them — God has ordained prayer as a means by which He fulfills His Word. (Ligonier: https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/delivered-assyrias-hand)

---

### v. 21 — *And the LORD sent an angel who annihilated every mighty man of valor... in the camp of the king of Assyria. So he withdrew... in disgrace. And when he entered the temple of his god, some of his own sons struck him down...*

- 2 Kings 19:35 gives the number: 185,000 Assyrian soldiers killed in one night. David Guzik compares this deliverance to the crossing of the Red Sea as "one of the two greatest examples of the Lord's intervention to save his people." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- The Targum says "the Word of the Lord sent Gabriel" to do this execution, and that it was done with lightning on the Passover night. (Matthew Henry: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- Gill notes some have speculated the angel used a natural means — "a hot pestilential wind, common in the eastern countries, called 'Samiel,' or the poison wind." Josephus took the angel to be the pestilence. Herodotus recorded a tradition that Sennacherib's camp was infested with mice/rats that destroyed the soldiers' arrows and shield-thongs — possibly a garbled version of the event. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm and Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- The Taylor Prism (Annals of Sennacherib, in the British Museum) confirms this event from the Assyrian side. Sennacherib boasts of taking 46 fortified cities and shutting up Hezekiah "like a bird in its cage" but notably never claims to have conquered Jerusalem — tacitly confirming the biblical account. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Sennacherib's death by his own sons (Adrammelech and Sharezer, Isaiah 37:38) occurred about 20 years later while worshiping in the temple of his god Nisroch. Poole notes: "God spared Sennacherib, not in mercy, but in wrath, reserving to him a more dreadful and shameful death by the hands of his own children." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Gill cites a Jewish legend (and emphasizes it is only a legend) that Sennacherib planned to sacrifice two sons to gain God's favor like Abraham, but the sons learned of it and killed him first. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)

---

### vv. 22–23 — *So the LORD saved Hezekiah and the people of Jerusalem... and He gave them rest on every side. Many brought offerings... and valuable gifts for Hezekiah... he was exalted in the eyes of all nations.*

- God not only saved Jerusalem from Assyria but also guided/guarded them "on every side" — like a shepherd leading his flock to safety. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- The influx of gifts to both the LORD (at the temple) and to Hezekiah parallels the fame of Solomon (cf. 2 Chronicles 9:23-24). Neighbouring nations recognized that the God of Israel had acted and sought His favour. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-32-commentary)
- Matthew Henry: "By the favour of God enemies are lost and friends gained." (Matthew Henry: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/32.htm)

---

### v. 24 — *In those days Hezekiah became mortally ill. So he prayed to the LORD, who spoke to him and gave him a sign.*

- The chronicler compresses what 2 Kings 20 and Isaiah 38–39 narrate in fuller detail. "In those days" likely places this illness around the time of the Assyrian crisis — perhaps about 712 BC, before the invasion of 701 BC, though interpreters debate the exact chronology. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- The "sign" was the retreating of the sundial's shadow by ten degrees (2 Kings 20:8-11; Isaiah 38:7-8). (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Gill refers readers to his commentary on Isaiah 38 for the full account of the sickness, prayer, and sign. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)

---

### vv. 25–26 — *But because his heart was proud, Hezekiah did not repay the favor shown to him. Therefore wrath came upon him... Then Hezekiah humbled the pride of his heart... so that the wrath of the LORD did not come upon them during the days of Hezekiah.*

- After miraculous deliverance from Assyria and healing from terminal illness, Hezekiah fell into pride. David Guzik notes this was not the pride of failing under weakness but the pride of failing under success — "Many men who stand strong against the temptations of failure and weakness fail under the temptations of success and strength." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- The specific act of pride was showing the Babylonian ambassadors all his treasures (v. 31; 2 Kings 20:12-19). Poole writes: "All which probably raised in him too great an opinion of himself… instead of walking humbly with God, and giving the glory all entirely to him, he took the honour to himself." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Knapp distinguishes this from Uzziah's pride: "It was not spiritual pride, as with his great-grandfather Uzziah; but worldly pride — 'the pride of life,' we might say." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Yet Hezekiah **humbled himself** — and remarkably, he led the inhabitants of Jerusalem to do the same. The result: wrath was deferred beyond his lifetime (though judgment eventually came in his descendants' days, Isaiah 39:6-7). (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- F.B. Meyer: "However pious and devoted a man may be, if he does not walk carefully, he will break down in some crucial test. It is easier to withstand the invasion of Sennacherib than the flattery of Babylon." (F.B. Meyer, cited at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/2-chronicles-32.html)
- Constable notes that Hezekiah "fell short of being the perfect Son of David, just like all the rest of Judah's monarchs. Yet when his heart did become proud because of God's blessings, he humbled himself. Consequently, God postponed His discipline." (Constable, cited at https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-32.html)

---

### vv. 27–29 — *Hezekiah had very great riches and honor... treasuries for silver, gold, precious stones, spices, shields... storehouses for grain and new wine and oil, stalls for livestock... for God gave him very great wealth.*

- Hezekiah's wealth was greatly increased by spoils from the Assyrian camp and presents from surrounding nations after the deliverance (v. 23). (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- The listing of treasuries, storehouses, and livestock parallels the description of Solomon's wealth and organization (cf. 2 Chronicles 9), presenting Hezekiah as a Solomonic figure enjoying divine blessing. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-32-commentary)
- Gill notes the Vulgate Latin reads "six cities" in some manuscripts for "he provided him cities" in v. 29. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)

---

### v. 30 — *It was Hezekiah who blocked the upper outlet of the Spring of Gihon and channeled it down to the west side of the City of David. And Hezekiah prospered in all that he did.*

- This refers to the famous **Hezekiah's Tunnel** — an extraordinary engineering achievement: a conduit cut through solid rock for 643 metres (covering a direct distance of 332 metres) to bring water from the Gihon Spring outside the city to the Pool of Siloam inside the walls. It was dug from both ends simultaneously and met in the middle. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- An inscription in cursive Hebrew (the **Siloam Inscription**, discovered in 1880) describes the tunnel's construction: "when the tunnel was driven through… the quarrymen hewed each towards the others, axe against axe. Then the waters flowed from the Spring to the Pool for 1,200 cubits." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Gill identifies Procopius Gazeus as equating Gihon with Siloam, and notes Maundrell's description of the pool of Gihon as "a stately pool, one hundred and six paces long, and sixty seven broad." (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- JFB describes Hezekiah's pool/reservoir within the northwest part of the city: "an oblong quadrangular tank, two hundred forty feet in length, from one hundred forty-four to one hundred fifty in breadth." (JFB: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-chronicles-32.html)

---

### v. 31 — *And so when ambassadors of the rulers of Babylon were sent to him to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land, God left him alone to test him, that He might know all that was in Hezekiah's heart.*

- The "wonder" (or sign) that drew the Babylonians was likely the sun's retrocession (the sundial going back ten degrees at Hezekiah's healing — Isaiah 38:7-8). Babylon was a center of astronomical study, so this phenomenon would have stirred intense curiosity. (JFB: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-chronicles-32.html and Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- JFB also suggests the Babylonians may have proposed a defensive alliance against Assyria. (JFB: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-chronicles-32.html)
- "God left him" (literally, "withdrew from him") — this is not divine abandonment but a deliberate test. God temporarily withdrew His restraining grace to reveal what was in Hezekiah's heart. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- Gill clarifies: "Not that God might know, who knows all things, unless spoken of him after the manner of men; but rather that Hezekiah might know the pride lurking in his heart… or that it might be known by others; that the children of men might know it." He cites Jeremiah 17:9 ("the heart is deceitful above all things"). (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- JFB pinpoints the core offense: "Hezekiah's offense was not so much in the display of his military stores and treasures, as in not giving to God the glory both of the miracle and of his recovery, and thus leading those heathen ambassadors to know Him." (JFB: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-chronicles-32.html)
- The full tragic consequences are spelled out in 2 Kings 20:16-18 — Isaiah prophesied that all the treasures Hezekiah showed would one day be carried off to Babylon. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)
- David Guzik's sober assessment: "God gave Hezekiah the gift of 15 more years of life, but the added years did not make him a better or a more godly man." (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)

---

### v. 32 — *As for the rest of the acts of Hezekiah and his deeds of loving devotion, they are indeed written in the vision of the prophet Isaiah... and in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.*

- "Vision of Isaiah" refers to the canonical book of Isaiah (called a "vision" in Isaiah 1:1). Much of Isaiah 36–39 parallels 2 Kings 18–20. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- The mention of "deeds of loving devotion" (*hesed*) highlights the Chronicler's positive overall assessment of Hezekiah. Despite his lapses, he was a king marked by covenant faithfulness. (Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-32-commentary)

---

### v. 33 — *And Hezekiah rested with his fathers and was buried in the upper tombs of David's descendants. All Judah and the people of Jerusalem paid him honor at his death. And his son Manasseh reigned in his place.*

- Hezekiah was buried "in the chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David" (KJV) — a place of highest honor among the royal tombs. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- Gill notes that some have identified grottos north of Jerusalem called "the sepulchres of the kings" as possibly Hezekiah's burial place, but acknowledges uncertainty. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- The honor shown at his death — great attendance at his funeral, burning of spices, and extended mourning — reflects how deeply the people esteemed him despite his late-life failures. (Gill: https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)
- The chapter ends with the ominous note that Manasseh — who would become Judah's most wicked king — succeeded him. The contrast is deliberate and sets up the theological tension of the next chapter. (Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)

---

## Summary of Distinctive Protestant Tradition Emphases

**Reformed/Presbyterian (Ligonier):** Emphasizes that Hezekiah had God's promise of deliverance through Isaiah yet still prayed — demonstrating that prayer is a divinely ordained means by which God fulfills His sure promises. God's sovereignty and human responsibility are held together. (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/delivered-assyrias-hand)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik):** Highlights the supernatural dimension — the angel of the Lord as a real being sent by God, the miraculous nature of the deliverance (185,000 killed in one night), and the "Satanic logic" of the enemy. The application emphasizes spiritual warfare and the personal reality of God's intervention. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-32/)

**Evangelical/Baptist (F.B. Meyer, Constable, Gill):** Stresses the compatibility of practical preparations with genuine faith ("pray to God and keep your powder dry"), the danger of pride after success, and that it is easier to withstand invasion than flattery. Gill (older Baptist-leaning) provides detailed linguistic and historical notes. Constable emphasizes the Chronicler's theology of retribution and how Hezekiah, while good, was not the perfect Son of David. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/2-chronicles-32.html , https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-32.html , https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/32.htm)

**Classic/Reformed (Matthew Henry, JFB, Morgan):** Matthew Henry draws extensive practical and devotional lessons, seeing in Sennacherib's letters the enduring pattern of Satan's attempts to destroy faith. JFB provides the strongest archaeological and geographical detail. Morgan emphasizes the seeming paradox that faithfulness invites trial — the Husbandman prunes the fruitful branch. (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/2_chronicles/32.htm , https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/2-chronicles-32.html)
